utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I continue my examination, I want to correct the record from something I said last week. I originally said that Prosecution Exhibit 505 had 12 tabs. That was an error. There are actually 17 tabs in that exhibit. And in the interest of saving time, the Prosecution will be withdrawing tab number 16. We will not work with it with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, we interrupted your testimony your last week with you describing when you received a DRS identification card, and you concluded your testimony by describing that that situation was not unique to yourself. I'd like to begin this morning by asking you: Were you aware of other officers that had dual forms of identification? And if so, can you describe the different types of identification that these other officers had.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as the military identification cards are concerned - and I'm talking about the senior officers of the Army of Republika Srpska who belonged to the 30th Personnel Centre - up until 1996 there was just the military ID card of the Yugoslav People's Army, and it was certified by the Army of Yugoslavia; whereas after 1996, what they introduced was an ID card of the Army of Republika Srpska. And from that time on, there were dual or double documents. Now, if there were any controls, then you knew which one you had to show. It was quite normal that in Republika Srpska you would show your ID issued by the authorities of the Army of Republika Srpska. And all the members and all the officers belonging to the 30th Personnel Centre did have this possibility. Now, in addition to that, you could also do the following: You had civilian documents, and we can deal with that later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to deal with that now. So you've described the situation with respect to military documents. My question to you is: Did members of the VRS born in Bosnia, living in Bosnia, did they also, to your knowledge, have civilian documentation identifying them as citizens of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, please? Do you mean the officers belonging to the 30th Personnel Centre or the officers who we can call conditionally Karadzic's officers? Which ones do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The officers of the 30th Personnel Centre, did they have civilian documentation identifying themselves as citizens of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The officers -- when I say "officers," actually I mean other categories of persons too, officers, non-commissioned officers, civilians working in the JNA, employed there, who later came -- became workers for the army, and for a time up to 1994 contractual staff too. So in addition to the documents that -- or rather, their civilian documents that could be issued in Republika Srpska, the other way they could go about this was to regulate their civilian documents in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In principle, this all boiled down to the fact that officers from one country couldn't be an officer until he had the citizenship of that particular country, state. And there was also the possibility after the war of settling your citizenship in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and by which you could take out an ID card and then table a request for citizenship to the Federal Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 505, tab 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you to take a look at this exhibit and ask you: Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise this document. This is a document which refers to the regulation of Yugoslav citizenship, what we were talking about a moment ago. And it specifies how one regulates Yugoslav citizenship issued by the command. I don't want to mention the number of the corps and the degree of confidentiality. It was issued, as is said here, by Colonel -- the colonel who signed the document. In principle, this relates to the regulation of Yugoslav citizenship for members of the 30th Personnel Centre on the basis of the law and documents of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, last week you testified that during your entire service assigned to a VRS unit, that you never received any pay from the VRS, that all of the pay came from the 30th Personnel Centre. My question to you today is: Were you aware of other officers in your unit that had the same arrangement? And if so, can you tell us how many or what percentage of officers in your unit had a similar arrangement with the 30th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the members of the 30th Personnel Centre, and the percentages in my unit, that number in principle ranged between -- or rather, went up to about 60 officers belonging to the 30th Personnel Centre; and are in the Army of Republika Srpska, that was five or six officers who were actually Karadzic's officers. I'd like to clarify one point: Karadzic's officers and the officers belonging to the 30th Personnel Centre, something in that regard, in the republic it was common knowledge among the people of what that difference was. So the officers who during the war were in Bosnia and underwent a shortened training programme were referred to as Karadzic's officers; whereas the officers who belonged to the 30th Personnel Centre were called Milosevic's officers. It's not quite logical because at that time the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was somebody else, in fact, and not Milosevic, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you just answer the questions that counsel asks you. If he wants an explanation, he'll -- he'll ask for it. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In addition to the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In addition to the officers that you describe as being paid through the 30th Personnel Centre, were there other types of staff in your unit that you are aware were paid for by the Army of Yugoslavia, the VJ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A large number of people who were in our units and appointed by order of the general staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please give us the categories of employees.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the categories of military employees are concerned belonging to the 30th Personnel Centre, let me take this in order. There were the officers, high-ranking officers and generals. Then there was the non-commissioned officers category, the NCOs; and the civilians employed in the JNA, which later became known as workers in the army. They, too, belonged there throughout that time - that is to say, belonged to the 30th Personnel Centre - and a certain number of soldiers who were there on a contract basis and who until the beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina had a signed contract with the then JNA. I should just like to emphasise in that regard that those contractual workers were taken off the list of the 30th Personnel Centre sometime in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, in your unit, what percentage of the entire staff of that unit was paid for by the Yugoslav army, or the VJ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the officers cadres, in my unit the number was over 90 per cent in view of the fact that this was a technical service of an army, branch of an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What percentage of the civilian staff in your unit, if you know, was made up of people paid for by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but what do you mean by "civilians"? Do you mean workers employed in the army? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct. The ones you referred to a moment ago. Are you able to say what percentage of those type of workers in your unit were paid for by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, that comes down to one category: All civilians employed in the JNA who until the 6th of April had employment in the Yugoslav People's Army, after the 6th of April became just workers in the army, and they were paid by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia still.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And these workers that you're now referring to, are these workers that remained in Bosnia after the JNA formally withdrew from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They remained in Bosnia after the withdrawal of the JNA, after the 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, without going into the circumstances under which you had an opportunity to see other people's personnel papers, did you have an opportunity to see the names or the personnel documents of other high-ranking members of the VRS that indicated to you that they were members also of the 30th Personnel Centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the members of the centre, of the 30th Personnel Centre, that is, the personnel administration and general staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, I can't establish the exact number, but I can say that it was a large number of persons. Colonel Lisica, the commander of the tactical operative group of Doboj, for example; General Talic, the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps and later chief of the Army of Republika Srpska, chief of staff; that and many others, so it's a large number. But for the most part, it refers to the officers who had worked for the JNA continued to work in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can now turn your attention to a slightly different topic. Can I ask you to give a brief explanation regarding how promotions operated, how the system of promotions operated with respect to members of the 30th Personnel Centre serving in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was promotion, another category, promotions for officers. And the promotion of officers who belonged to the 30th Personnel Centre and were located in the Army of Republika Srpska was conducted in Belgrade on the basis of the service itself, their service, and this was a factual promotion. There was the possibility of promotions pursuant to the president of Republika Srpska, Radovan Karadzic's requests, but in the material sense, until that rank and title is verified by the Army of Yugoslavia, the person -- the promotion in question was -- did not come into effect, to all intents and purposes, because the moneys received by an officer on the basis of his rank was determined by the Army of Yugoslavia, so that in practice what happened was that the possibility existed that in the Army of Republika Srpska an individual - for example, a general - was being paid by the army as he would be for the rank of colonel. So until the Army of Yugoslavia certified and verified that rank, he would receive the former salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that you take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 505, tab 10. And ask you: Do you recognise what this document is? And if so, can you please summarise it briefly for us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do recognise this document. I know what is contained in it, what it's about, and it refers to what we were talking about a moment ago. And in this particular case, it refers to a certain general for recognition of the right to a salary group, and that group is PG4, and confirmation --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you to tell us what is the general's name who is the subject of this document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the request by General Stanislav Galic for recognition of the right to salary group PG4 and confirmation of the rank of lieutenant general. The document was signed by the chief of the general staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, Major General Pero Colic, and it was sent to the personnel administration of the general staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the chief of staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska is in essence requesting the 30th Personnel Centre, or the Yugoslav army, to do what with respect to General Galic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this gentleman, actually Major General Pero Colic, this is a request, this document is been tabled in the form of a request. And he is reporting and requesting that General Stanislav Galic be given recognition for the PG4 salary group instead of the number 6 group that he previously had, in order to regulate his pension, retirement benefits, and so on. So the level of salary groups goes from a higher level to a lower level. From officers, it ranges from group 21 downwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to now ask you to read a portion of that document. If I could just draw your attention to the second paragraph where it says -- beginning with, "The decrees were issued by the responsible superior officer in the conformity with the regulations of the Army of Yugoslavia which were valid at the time they were issued." Perhaps instead of asking you to read that, could I ask you to comment on that sentence. Does that indicate that promotions were regulated -- promotions of officers in the VRS serving in the 30th Personnel Centre were regulated by the law governing the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were regulated by the law governing the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to now ask you to take a look at several documents belonging to personnel folders of some other prominent members of the VRS and ask for your brief comment on them. I would first turn your attention to Prosecution Exhibit 505, tab 11. And if I could draw the Chamber's attention to the first green tag in that tab. And my question to you with respect to this document: Is this another year-of-service form similar to the year-of-service form that we discussed at length in your testimony last week with respect to yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is another example of the year-of-service form --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for pension insurance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does this relate to a person by the name of Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does relate to Obrenovic, son of Milomir, a major working at the military post. And this is the document regulating his years of service and pensionable service years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And does it indicate whether or not he received double credit in the army -- while serving in Bosnia, whether he received double credit towards his pension with the Yugoslav army, the VJ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, under point 2, we see the calculations for the length of service following the 12/24 formula relating to the years of service of officers during wars.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, members of the 30th Personnel Centre serving in Bosnia, did they have the right to military housing in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as that is concerned, certain persons regulated their housing in the Army of Yugoslavia. Some regulated it within Republika Srpska. And in principle, that didn't mean that all the members of the 30th cadre centre had it in one or the other form. But it is important to state that those who did not have their housing problems regulated would receive remuneration and an added sum of money to cater to their housing costs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: They would receive that remuneration from which army, the VRS or the VJ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Army of Yugoslavia. All payments to members of the 30th Personnel Centre came from the Army of Yugoslavia, were regulated through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that the witness be shown tab 11 of Prosecution Exhibit 505. And if I could draw the Chamber's attention to the blue tag.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And my question to you, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can I just deal with one very small matter, indeed --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- but it can go very wrong. Until two weeks ago, exhibits produced by the Prosecution were simply referred to as exhibits, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. as I recollect. And two weeks ago, for some reason a new regime was introduced, without consultation, where Prosecution exhibits suddenly were called Prosecution Exhibits and marked with a P. Now, that, I would suggest, is going to lead to great confusion because after more than a year we suddenly have a new marking. Now, you must go back to the old system and mark the exhibits simply as exhibits and Defence Exhibits will be given a D number, the Prosecution will simply have a number. And it would be helpful if you would bear that in mind, Mr. Groome, in referring to these exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, no need to apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I ask you to take a look at this exhibit. Is this a document with respect to Major Obrenovic's housing situation as regulated by the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is also a request by Major Obrenovic from which we can see that he had requested that his housing problems be resolved, and the request was addressed to the command of the town of Novi Sad in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And it was signed by Lieutenant Colonel Gojko Mijic of -- head of the personnel centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I can turn your attention to Exhibit 505, tab 11. And this would be the first red tag, to assist the Chamber, in the particular document of this tab. Sir, I ask you to take a look at this document. I ask you: Do you recognise it, and can you summarise it for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have in my hand order number BP/5/2/150 of the commander of the 5th Corps, dated the 29th of September, 1998. It deals with the appointment of Milomir Obrenovic, a Lieutenant Colonel of the armoured mechanised unit. And he's appointed commander of the 503rd motorised brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to read you one sentence of that document and ask you to explain its meaning to the Chamber. I'm quoting from the document: "Currently under RF and MF, deputising for the commander of the 503rd Motorised Brigade in the VJ ground forces 30th Personnel Centre Corps." My question to you is: The 503rd Motorised Brigade, in which army did that motorised brigade belong?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 503rd Motorised Brigade belonged to the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the phrase "VJ ground forces 30th Personnel Centre Corps," which army is that referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It refers to 30th Personnel Centre of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I could ask that the witness be shown document -- or Exhibit 505, tab 11. And this would be the second red tab. And for the record, the ERN number ends in 6839.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if I could draw your attention to the first sentence in that document: "I accepted my duty as a commander of the 503rd Motorised Brigade in the 5th Corps in the 30th Personnel Centre in the Yugoslav army general staff." This is a letter signed by Lieutenant Colonel Dragan Obrenovic. Can you please explain the first sentence in that letter. Where exactly is Lieutenant Colonel Obrenovic assigned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the takeover of duty by the commander of the 503rd Motorised Brigade in the 5th Corps in the 30th Personnel Centre in the general staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, where exactly is the location of the unit, the date when the duty was taken over, and signed in person by Lieutenant Colonel Dragan Obrenovic. Forwarded also to the personnel administration of the general staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and the financial body. The stamp of the command of the 5th Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn to the personnel folder or personnel documents from the file of Lieutenant Vinko Pandurevic. And the first document I'd ask you to look at is document 505, tab 12. And the Chamber -- it's been marked by a red tab that is ERN number ending 0337. Last week you identified a document regulating your pension rights with respect to your service. Is this document a similar document with respect to Lieutenant Vinko Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. In this case, this is a document of the general staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. It relates to Lieutenant Colonel Vinko Pandurevic, whereby a decision is being taken to recognise double credit for years of service from 1992 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature on the bottom of that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the signature of Colonel Ljubomir Lalic, who was in the 30th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is he the person who signed many of your personnel documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All documents were signed by Ljubomir Lalic or Gojko Mijic, who both worked in the 30th Personnel Centre. When I say that they worked there, I mean that they actually worked in the 30th Personnel Centre in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I can turn your attention to another document in tab 12, and this is ERN number ending 9019, and it's marked by a green tag in the -- the binders distributed to the Chamber and to the amici and the accused. Is this another example of a Years of Service form, the type which you've described in detail last week?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is another example for Vinko Pandurevic - in this case, it says "Major" - regulating his retirement benefit, and on the basis of the previous decision, we see that he is recognised double credit for years of service as of 1992. Signed by the 30th Personnel Centre, Belgrade, by -- and signed by Colonel Ljubomir Lalic and registered in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The final document I'd ask you to comment on from this tab is ERN ending 0095, and it's marked by a blue tag in the binders distributed in the court here. Can I ask you: Do you recognise this document? And if so, can you briefly summarise what is contained in this document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is an order 2-252 dated the 31st of December, 1995. It deals with the promotion of Lieutenant Colonel Vinko Pandurevic to the rank of infantry colonel. And it is indicated that he is employed in the 30th Personnel Centre of the general staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and the date of the promotion. Underneath, we also see the promotion to the rank of major, the colonel of armoured mechanised units, that is, Dragan Obrenovic also serving in the 30th Personnel Centre of the general staff of the Yugoslavia army, and he's being promoted on such and such a date, military post Zvornik. And registered in the military post at Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that the witness now be shown Exhibit 505, tab 13. The ERN ends in 0732, and it's marked by a red tag.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, if I could just ask you to briefly comment. This is a personnel document belonging to Colonel Jovo Kundacina. Is this another example of a member of the 30th Personnel Centre having his pension rights regulated by the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This is a decision recognising for Colonel Jovo Kundacina double years of service as of the 20th of May, 1992. And it is signed by Colonel Ljubomir Lalic from the 30th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I can ask you to look at document 505 -- in 505 -- Exhibit 505, tab 14, ERN ending 9459. It's marked by a green tag. Is this another example of a Years of Service form? If you can just briefly tell us yes or no and the name of the person who this pertains to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is another document recognising for this particular officer -- this is a retirement form from which one can see the period for which double credit is given, and that is for the years of service during wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe the -- can you tell us the years or the period during which this person received double credit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For this person, for this military officer, the wartime double credit is given from the 25th of July, 1992 until the 9th of November, 1993, because the decision was written in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was signed by Colonel Ljubomir Lalic in the 30th Personnel Centre of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the only other document in this particular tab I'd ask you to look at ends in ERN number 9461, and it's marked by a red tag. Can I ask you: Do you recognise this document? Can you please summarise what this document is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the same person, and a certificate is being issued to him. This is a certificate showing that this person has been transferred and appointed to a duty in military post 3001 Belgrade where he performed tasks in the zone of combat operations from the 25th of July, 1992. And it is intended for regulating double years of service, and it is signed by the commander, Lieutenant Colonel Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the final set of documents or personnel records from the 30th Personnel Centre I'd ask you to look at are contained in tab 15 of Exhibit 505. You mentioned earlier today about promotions occurring both in the VRS but finally being recognised in the 30th Personnel Centre of the Yugoslav army. I would ask you to take a look at these documents and ask you to -- to describe what is contained in these documents.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have here an extract from the order of the command of the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, whereby Zoran Mandic is promoted to the rank of lieutenant, but promotion was written by Lieutenant General Ratko Mladic, and it is certified by Lieutenant Colonel Mile Negovanovic, or confirmed by Mile Negovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What is the date of that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at another document from that same tab, ending in ERN number 4829. It's dated the 7th of January, 1993. Can I ask you to describe what's contained in that document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, Your Honours, this is the same sort of document, only this latter document is an extract from order 3-3 of the chief of staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, whereby the same person is being promoted to the same rank. The difference being that it was signed by the chief of staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, a Lieutenant General Momcilo Perisic. And the promotion applies to the same date, the 20th of July, 1992, which means that this rank has been verified, or this act of promotion has been verified by the Yugoslav army. The person bearing a certain rank in the Army of Republika Srpska, that rank was verified on his payment slip. He's being paid on the basis of that rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the final set of documents I'm going to ask you to comment on in your testimony this morning are contained in Exhibit 505, tab 17. I'm going to ask that you be shown the two documents in that -- or I ask that you be shown the document ending in 1850. Can I ask you to describe -- first of all, the heading of that reads "Military post 4001 Belgrade." Can I ask you to describe what that military post is and describe what is contained in this document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 30th Personnel Centre was organised for the territory of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina. Similarly, the territory of Croatia under Serbian control had organised a 40th Personnel Centre, and this is a document of that kind issued by military post 4001 Belgrade, which means the 40th Personnel Centre. And in this, Milan Celeketic, father's name Pero, in the service at the military post 4001, which means the 40th Personnel Centre, and who is on duty in the military post 9000 Knin. And this has to do with recognition of rights or entitlements on the basis of aggravated circumstances, that is, an increased amount in relation to his basic salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can ask you now to take a look at the other document in that tab, ending ERN 1853. And the first question I would ask you regarding this document is: Do you recognise the signature of this document from the 40th Personnel Centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do recognise the signature. It is the person who signed my documents as well, and that is Colonel Ljubomir Lalic, and his signature, the man employed in the 30th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, during the time, the period of time between 1992 to 1995 during which you served in Bosnia as a member of the 30th Personnel Centre, did you consider yourself to be a member -- or you considered yourself to be a member of which army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the wartime period, from 1992 to 1995, on all the grounds that constitute the position of an officer, rank, and promotion, and all my duties and rights, I considered myself and the rest of us as members of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the final matter that I would seek to put to this witness, I'd ask that a video be marked for identification. The Prosecution will be tendering it through a witness next week. But because of this witness's expertise, he will be able to identify a small portion of that video, so I would ask that it be given a number for identification and that a few seconds of it be played for this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 506, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you to look at the video screen before you, and it will go by rather quickly. So I'd ask the director to now play it. After it finishes, I'd ask you to describe, if you can, identify the type of helicopter shown by the instrument panel that you can see in this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, can you identify the type of helicopter by the instrument panel that we could see in this portion of video?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is the Gazelle-type helicopter, and every corps commander had one such helicopter which was used by the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when you say "corps commander," are these corps commanders of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All corps commanders had at their disposal a helicopter, and a pilot was allotted for that helicopter from the air force to serve for the needs of the corps commander of the ground forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 127, I see from your statement that you are no longer an officer, you are no longer a member of the army. Tell me, when did you leave the Army of Republika Srpska? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding when I left the Army of Republika Srpska, I was there throughout the time of the war, partly after the war. I lived through all of that. As for the actual date when I left, in view of the fact that it relates to my personal career, could I not answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell us roughly. What year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the moral standpoint, the ethical standpoint, I was a member of the army and I performed all assignments given to me and even after the bombing by NATO forces in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So until 1999, you were in the Army of Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was -- I remained in the Army of Yugoslavia right up until the point when there was the slightest hope of some sort of Yugoslavia. Unfortunately, today Yugoslavia is dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I'm asking you, when did you abandon the Army of Republika Srpska? You were there throughout the war. I'm asking you a simple question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've given you an answer. I was a member even after the NATO airstrikes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Okay. We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said you were an atheist, and in terms of ethnicity, what are you? Tell me, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as my ethnicity or nationality, for a long time, according to my papers, I was a Muslim. But in every real sense, I was a Yugoslav and my homeland was the former Yugoslavia, and remained my homeland.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm glad to see you here, because even as a Muslim in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, during the war you remained first in the Army of Yugoslavia and then in the Army of Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that I was a Muslim did not affect my decision to stay in any way. I always supported those who supported Yugoslavia in any form. But the most honest part of it was Yugoslavia for everyone. Unfortunately, I have to say in hindsight that Yugoslavia does not exist and nobody gave any thought to the people who felt as real Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, those who broke up Yugoslavia didn't give any thought to these people, not those who wanted to preserve it. But please, tell me: Was there anyone in all those years that you spent first in the JNA, then in the Army of Republika Srpska, was there anyone who forced you from one army to another?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could you define "forcing" and "from one army to another"; what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone force you into the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as that is concerned, we could say that it was such a combination of circumstances that made me stay in the Army of Republika Srpska as a member of the 30th Personnel Centre. Most of those who left the then-JNA - and I'm now speaking of Muslims and Croats - I stayed, for instance, I remained, hoping that sooner or later some sort of Yugoslavia will prevail, a homeland for everyone. But I regret to say once again it doesn't exist any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I regret that too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand we are in open session. Is that right, Mr. May? That's all I wanted to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 3, paragraph 2, you say that since you were not a Serb, you were excluded from the majority of sensitive activities performed by your unit. And you say that Serbs treated you with suspicion. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in view of the fact that I did not clearly belong to the Serb people in terms of ethnicity, I was not fit for performing special tasks, confidential tasks, everything that is subject to some sort of confidentiality and protection, although technically speaking I executed all my orders, and appearing here I'm only talking about things that I have seen myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, regarding what I quoted from your statement, namely that you were excluded from most sensitive activities of your unit, are you talking about the period when you were still an officer of the JNA or the period when you became an officer of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am talking about the period when I -- not became an officer of the Army of Republika Srpska, because we wore insignia of that army but I have to tell you once again, we were members of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I always stick to the rules, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said you had no access to certain affairs in your unit and you were assigned to various administrative duties in the barracks; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this term "administrative duties" is not quite accurate. Those are auxiliary duties, support duties, except -- apart from the basic duties of the unit, every member has auxiliary duties related to quartermaster issues and various other things every officer must know and do. But as for the 30th Personnel Centre, I don't know what the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You will answer that question when I ask it. And we'll take explanations in the order which I see fit. So please just answer my questions. You claim, however --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lest we have to go into closed session again, Mr. May, on page 3, paragraph 2, this witness even quotes the date when he was already an officer of the Army of Republika Srpska, when he said that he was transferred to the place where he was transferred in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that he was appointed to a position within the unit whose number I will not read, and that unit had the highest ranking in terms of secrecy -- that position had the highest ranking in terms of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. secrecy and confidentiality. You can read exactly what this position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any position within that unit that you could have possibly been appointed to and that involved more confidentiality and secrecy? If you want us to move into closed session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Private session again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, from your statement, Mr. 127, without mentioning any ranks, because I don't want to be accused of identifying you by doing so, but during the period of time that you're testifying about, from 1991 to 1997, in fact, there were four ranks which you received; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was given four ranks. They were regular promotions which I received. So -- do I have the floor? Yes. These were ranks, captain in 1994, for example, or in 1997 was the next rank up the ladder. They were regular promotions which did not have any great bearing on the fact that actually I had done anything extra to deserve those promotions. Otherwise, they would have been extraordinary promotions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, are you saying that during that period of time, covering six years, you moved up the ranks, four ranks, in fact, because somebody was discriminated, like yourself, as you say? So you received four high ranks and yet you were somebody who was not greatly trusted. You received four ranks, went up the ladder four times during those years?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think the witness has claimed that he was subject to discrimination. That was your expression.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the witness said that in view of the fact that he wasn't a Serb, he was excluded from most of the sensitive activities. Much of the more sensitive activity. And we have observed, therefore, on the basis of his own statements and the facts presented here for him and by him, that over a period of six years he received six ranks or six promotions -- four promotions. I'm sorry, four ranks and promotions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And my question is the following: As for a time you were a JNA officer, usually how long do you have to spend in one rank to be promoted to a higher rank? For example, a lieutenant, how long does he have to stay in the rank of lieutenant before he becomes a captain or from captain move on to captain first class? The public is listening to you. There are many soldiers in the audience and they know about all this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what you say is correct. But it wasn't four ranks up the ladder within a space of six years. When an officer completes military academy - we're talking about regular promotions - when he becomes an officer, it depends on how long his training in the military academy lasted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Stop interrupting. Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, after the first year, he receives a regular rank of lieutenant; having spent three years of service, he becomes a captain; after the next three years, he becomes captain first class. So they weren't four ranks; it was the regular system moving up the ladder of ranks, nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how many years do you have to add up three plus three plus three? How many years go by from captain to major? Do you mean to say that after every three years you go up automatically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have to spend three to five years working in a single rank. That was the law. And as far as promotions are concerned, let me state at the outset that this had no bearing -- or rather, they were regular promotions. Had there been any extraordinary promotions, then it would have said so in the document: So and so is being extraordinarily promoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you just said you had to spend between three and five years working in one rank, and you received all these ranks within the space of just six years. Therefore, I can't see from what I'm looking at here that there was -- you were hampered in any way in your military promotions, but quite the reverse seems to have taken place. In fact, you moved up the ranks very speedily; isn't that right, Mr. 127?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as moving up the ranks is concerned, let me state again that this was a normal legal way in which this happened. And all officers from my particular generation would receive their ranks regularly at the same time, of a generation. So this was not any special merit on my part. It was just my generation being moved up the ranks. For example, the class of 1939 would this year gain the rank of such and such, and you can look at that if you look at the date when I graduated from the military academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 127, as we can see here that the reverse took place, that you moved up the ranks very speedily, tell me now, why are you claiming that you were subjected to problems or subjected to lack of trust because you were not a Serb? Why are you claiming that now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you what I experienced, and I know what I went through myself; as for this wariness that people had towards me and other things too, the assignment of certain duties, carrying them out, additional duties such as being duty officer in a barracks, and things like that in addition to our regular job, what we had been trained and educated to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. 127, I'm not a professional soldier. I was a reserve officer. And all officers have to perform their -- the work of a duty officer in barracks, for example, along the regular lines of duty, except for the chief of staff and commander. Is there any other soldier that does not at one time or another have duty work to perform in a barracks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No question in this, mere statement. We will adjourn now, 20 minutes, and we'll continue thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have an hour and 50 minutes left with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood it, Mr. May, that I have to the end of the day, in view of the fact that the witness testified quite some time before the break and this morning, almost an hour this morning and before we adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We considered that, and the time available for you, is, as I say, 1 hour, 50 minutes. That's allowing for the time which he had with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll do my best to cover the ground as quickly as possible, but it seems to me that the time for examination-in-chief was longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 127, in your statement you quoted the names - and I'm not going to read the names out, so we don't have to move into private session - but you stated the names, first and last names, of all your superiors, commanding officers, at the time when you were in the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is correct. That is the pre-war chain of command for me onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We can see from that, without reading the name, that the commander of your company was a Croat; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And I'm talking about the times of the JNA, when everybody was in the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the battalion commander was a Muslim, is that right, too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, that is correct. But as I say, we're talking about peacetime establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the commander of the 5th Corps of the RViPVO was a Croat; is that right? The air force and air defence commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But you skipped over a person in the chain of command who was a Serb. Let's not skip people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So apart from one man - and that's what I was getting to, and I don't want to read out that man's name, who was a Serb - all your other superior officers belonged to other ethnicities; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the period of time we're talking about, this wasn't essential. It didn't matter who was what, because we're talking about the times of the Yugoslav People's Army, where nobody paid attention to names but to capability and ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Now, did you have any problems at that time for not being a Serb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, as I say, during the time of the Yugoslav People's Army, I had no problems. I was a happy man. I loved my homeland, my country, a country for one and all, for all the nationalities or ethnic groups living within it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2, paragraph 3, when you speak about the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina, you state that all supersonic planes of the MiG type were displaced from Bosnia-Herzegovina, were moved out of there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, that those types of planes were transferred to Yugoslavia, the MiG jets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, why do you say almost all of them, almost all MiG jets? I assume you know that not a single MiG stayed on in Republika Srpska, was left there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, not a single MiG, either 21 or 29-type jet, was left in the territory controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then we've established that. Now, on that same page, in that same paragraph, you go on to say that the light planes of Yugoslavia, during the no-fly zone, violated the air space above Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but could you repeat that? You said light planes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, on that same page, same paragraph, you say that the planes, light planes of the Army of Yugoslavia in 1995, during the no-fly zone period, violated the air space above Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about light aircraft which violated the air space above Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me, which light aircraft were these?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were non-combat aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's sufficient. That's enough. I've heard what I need. So it was non-combat planes, non-combat aircraft. And they did not open fire on any territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't able to see whether they went into action and targeted anything or whether they were just reconnoitring. Reconnoitring and reconnaissance is also part of combat operations if you're flying over a territory. And if a plane takes off, for example, from an airport outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, you are in fact violating the air space of Bosnia-Herzegovina flying over it, or Republika Srpska. And if the plane goes back and lands from the spot he took off, then that's it. And in view of the speed and all the rest of it, you can determine which type of aircraft was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you said non-combat aircraft. Now, how many violations, how many instances of this kind of violation took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know but it happened from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, why are you mentioning that at all? If some non-combat aircraft on the border regions violated the no-fly zone along the edges, the ridges, is that some kind of criminal activity of its own, in its own, or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, I was not able to establish the assignment, what the purpose of the flight in question was, the flyovers, whether they were engaged in any combat activity, whether it was reconnaissance or whatever and -- or whether it was a wholly non-combat flight taking place, as you yourself say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as you're talking about 1995 and violations of the air space above Bosnia-Herzegovina, do you happen to know of any violations in 1995, not only of the air space but also general violations from some other party or side, that is to say, not coming from Yugoslavia? Did anything of that kind take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific, explain what you mean for me to be able to speak about concrete violations about -- from another side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I assume you've heard of the village of Svodna near Prijedor. It's not far from Banja Luka either, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you remember that it was precisely in 1995 that due to the effects of the MiG planes belonging to the Croatian air force, that a number of people were killed? They were killed on the spot, and everybody from the village of Slavno Polje Vrginmost had to -- I'm sure you would have known that and seen it; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The violation of air space from the territory of the Republic of Croatia, that also did exist, but I didn't testify about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't matter whether you spoke of it or not. I'm asking you a question. Were there combat operations and did -- were people killed? And I quoted the example of the village of Svodna, right next to Prijedor, when people were killed, because the Croatian air force went into operation there. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information as to whether or how many people were killed, I really can't say. Now, that there were violations of the air space, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know that they went into operation and targeted targets, these aircraft, Croatian aircraft targeted places?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every combat flight, whether fire is opened on targets or whether control, supervision, and reconnoitring is going on, each flight is a combat flight and each flight is seen to be a violation of the air space if it takes place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But this wasn't only a violation of the air space, was it? It was opening fire on targets and the killing of people as a result. And I assume that not even according to your own criteria is that the same thing. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that the air force did enter into combat. Now, whether there was anybody who was killed, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was in command of the Croatian air force in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who was in command in those days? Well, logically, it must have been one of the commanders who used to be in the former JNA. Now, who exactly it was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know that Imre Agotic, a general, was in command? Just say "I know" or "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about Imre Agotic. He was commander and he was a highly appreciated officer of the Croatian army, very highly thought of. I even heard that he was close to the former president, Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that he issued orders for the engagement of the planes of the Croatian air force that I referred to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A logical consequence of everything. That is, if he was the commander, then he probably issued orders. But as I was saying, I can't talk about that. I could only perhaps notice violations of the air space. But it's only logical to suppose that orders were issued by a commander. Now, whether it is Imre Agotic or some other officer, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In August 1995, immediately after this Croatian operation, were you still working at your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, immediately after the Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was saying, very few data were accessible, but what I know, I will say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were operations against the refugee column when a number of civilians were dismembered in the immediate vicinity of Bosanski Petrovac, a number of civilians? I assume you know the area. They were dismembered by bombs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was in Banja Luka. But people who were working with me at the time, who were on duty, I heard from them that there had been certain operations. Now, what the consequences were, I really didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know that they targeted the refugee column.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear of it. But as I was saying, I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you hear of the targeting of Croatian planes on ambulances and a hospital close to Dragotina village on the border between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard quite -- of a about -- I heard about a number of events during the withdrawal of the army, the Serbian army of Krajina, the withdrawal of the refugees. And to be quite frank, it wasn't nice to look at for anyone, let me make myself quite clear. And we can only talk about what actually happened. In 1995, it was dreadful to watch those refugee columns because every mother cries for her children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you are aware of Croatian action, air force action against those refugee columns, including Red Cross, ambulances, and hospitals.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it from other people, that the air force did operate, but in those days I was not operationally involved, and I cannot claim that this happened. I only heard it from others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in 1994 the Croatian air force also shelled a Serbian village, Batusa, near Vrginmost, in the immediate vicinity of the border with Bosnia-Herzegovina? Do you remember that event? Because it was in an area which you must have had access to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were violations of air space in Bosnia-Herzegovina by the Croatian air farce.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But do you know, as it was shelled, bombed, by the air force, this Serbian village, that a Croatian pilot, Peric [phoen], piloted that plane who was shot down immediately after that operation, near Dubo Selo [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the specific details about certain operations on the part of the Croatian army. I didn't have access or insight. As regards violations of the air space, however, and operations by the air force, because planes won't fly for nothing; as soon as they violate the air space, it means that they did engage. But I can't assert anything about the consequences of those engagements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it beyond dispute that all those actions took place in the no-fly zone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The no-fly zone, as we know, was in force throughout. Now, as I was saying, regarding what happened, if there were violations, were there counteractions by units within the operation of no-fly zones, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware, for instance -- so what I'm going to ask you now, that in 1991 and the SFRY and the JNA were still in existence, following orders by General Jurevic, who was then the commander -- and he was a Croat, of course. You remember that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In order to deblock the Mekusa [phoen] and Glogovica barracks near Karlovac, two planes took off from the Bihac airport in 1991. Do you remember that, two MiG planes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about the Karlovac barracks blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. To deblock the barracks by order of General Jurevic, two MiG planes took off from the Bihac airport, to deblock these two barracks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a lot of activity from the Bihac airport in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it is known that one of those planes, and not by error, opened fire on the barracks itself, when several JNA soldiers were killed, and a second one opened fire on paramilitary forces that were holding the barracks under siege. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was saying, in that period I had no control. I know that there was such activities, that there was opening fire on one's own forces. I am saying that in those days whether it was an intentional error or an error by General Jurevic, I cannot establish at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've stopped your microphone because there are difficulties caused by your overlapping, both the witness and the accused cross-examining. Witness B-127, could you bear this in mind, please: Because we have this special microphone for you and voice distortion, it's most important that you don't reply to any question until it's over. So would you keep an eye on the microphone in front of the accused. And when the light is off, start replying. And Mr. Milosevic, would you bear in mind the need for a pause after the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that this MiG landed in Zagreb and it was piloted by a JNA pilot, a Croat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of another case when a plane fled from Ponikve and landed in Austria. It was a case of defection. Maybe this case occurred, but I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: About the case that you are aware of, one landed in Klagenfurt in Austria, is that right, one of those two planes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it took off from Ponikve.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Austrian authorities handed over both the pilot and the plane to the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite possible. But I really don't know whether they handed them over to the Republic of Croatia, if not to the Army of Yugoslavia. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So you don't know. Let us then move on about what you do know. On page 2, paragraph 4, and page 3, paragraph 1, you say that after May 1992, upon the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina, certain reports relating to the air force were submitted to the operations centre in Banja Luka, and from there on to the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, let us look, please, as instructions were presented here for command and cooperation between the air defences and air force support -- it says, "Approved commander by the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, Lieutenant General Ratko Mladic."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbian version of this document is 00876254, the title page -- and the English version, Mr. May, 03014149, title page. This is quite a lengthy document --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- which Mr. Groome presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't catch that, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The accused is referring to tab 4 of Exhibit 505.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Has the witness got the document? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it's a document approved by the Commander of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska, Lieutenant General Ratko Mladic in those days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is what it says in the top left-hand corner. And the document was signed, as far as I can see, because some pages of my copy are empty and some are printed - so let me just find it - signed by chief of staff, I assume, of the PVO of the Army of Republika Srpska, Jovan Maric. And we can see here also the stamp of the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please go back to the first page. And let's take chapter 2, where it says, "A decision on the opening of fire on targets in the air space --" in brackets it says "VAP." Now, what does that mean? In the air space, doesn't it, VAP -- "is made by the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska for all PVO forces for the war zone of the VRS"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then it goes on to say, "In keeping with this decision, the commanders of the corps and the air force and anti-air defences of the Army of Republika Srpska shall through their operative centres issue individual orders for the opening of fire on identified enemy aircraft." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then it says, "Fire shall be opened without any special order from the operative centre of the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and the operative centre of the air force and anti-air defences and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the operative centre of the corps on all targets in the area which attack elements of combat disposition and other facilities." Is that what it says, Mr. 127?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then, "The distribution of targets between LA and RJ --" what does LA and RJ and PVO ARJ stand for? -- "directly through the operative centre of the corps of the Army of Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means what will be assigned to fighter aircraft, what to lighter aircraft, and to artillery units; which targets are assigned to which units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So directly through the operative centre of the PVO and the ViPVO, these stand for the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And a ban on opening fire shall be issued by the operative centre of the ViPVO through the operative centres of the corps; is that right? In order to secure overflights by our aircraft, a ban on opening fire. Then second paragraph: "Coordinated action between VRS and PVO units," these all refer to units of the Army of Republika Srpska. And it goes on to say: "Where fighter aircraft are free to act --" this is again a reference to the Army of Republika Srpska, isn't it, Mr. 127? Then in item 2, halfway down, you see, "Coordination between Vojin elements shall be effected through the system of surveillance, warning and guidance for the purpose of control of the air space of Republika Srpska and approaches to it."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Within the unified system of control of the air space.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The air space of Republika Srpska and approaches to it; correct? And then it goes on to discuss the situation in the air space and so on and so forth, and it keeps referring to the Army of Republika Srpska. And then you have item 3, which you discussed -- referred to in your diagram, about some alleged connection with the Army of Yugoslavia. And then subheading 3, "Coordinated action between the air force and air defence and the air force and air defence of the Yugoslav army and that of the Army of Serbian Krajina." This item 3 is the shortest one and it discusses exclusively the exchange of information. Is that correct, Mr. 127?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: The task of those units is also to collect information and to provide it to interested parties, users. Just a moment. The task of those units is to detect and identify aircraft in air space, and this information is to be provided to users, be it fighter aviation or rocket, that is, missile units of the air defence centre. So that is their combat assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it clear that only this item 3, related to the exchange of information, deals with the exchange of information with certain elements who also collect information for the Army of Yugoslavia, that is, their counterpart, which also collects information for the Army of Yugoslavia and exchanges it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is clearly defined here. This instruction defines also a coordinated action with the units of Army of Yugoslavia and the units which have the same task for the air space of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They perform the task of air surveillance, warning, and guidance, that is, radar service and collection of information; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a combat assignment too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But their only task is to act in coordination with the Army of Yugoslavia, limited to exchanging information about the air space.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says precisely, "Exchange of information, specifying the level of exchange with units located both within the Army of Yugoslavia and in the Serbian Army of Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the nature of these special units is exclusively to collect and exchange information; correct or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you, this is the task of one unit within the army, to collect information. Please let me finish. Once again, to identify targets, to see whether it's hostile or our own target, to provide information to the unit which will intervene, depending on the decision of the commander, whether to shoot down the plane or to make it land, to alert the civilian population to air danger. All this information is received from these units, and it is within their combat assignments to inform all interested parties, users of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us look for a moment at this diagram that you provided. I don't suppose you will put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was dealt with in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll go into closed session, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I mean, tab 3. Do you want to ask any questions about this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing for private session. I only wanted to point out the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only link --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We dealt with it in private session, so we will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, tab 3 is under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness have a copy in front of him.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So since we established that this item 3, dealing with the exchange of information with the Army of Yugoslavia, effected through radio relay links about the situation in air space, serving the purpose of air space protection, is the only type of collaboration indicated here. I would now like to point out to chapter 5 of this same instruction, dealing with the application and specification of this instruction, application and elaboration of instructions. In your version, it's page 8, chapter 8, application and elaboration of the instructions. Sentence number 2 -- I can actually read the entire paragraph. "Commands of the corps and the air force and air defence --" air force and air defence meaning those of Republika Srpska; correct? Correct, Mr. 127?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Based on this instruction, they will elaborate on and link up PVO forces in their zone of responsibility. And now the main sentence: "The command of the air defence and air force shall analyse all matters from chapter 2, item 3 of the instructions with the air force and air defence command of the Army of Yugoslavia." So that is the type of links from item 3 that I just quoted to you, and there is no other coordinated action except in terms of exchanging information. Isn't that clear from this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that we can see clearly from these instructions that two systems are acting in coordination; the systems of air defence in Republika Srpska and the one in Yugoslavia, and I only specified at which level it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Certainly, because in chapter 2, item 3 is the only one that deals with this. And item 3 relates only to exchange of information. Whereas, item 5 says that they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're wasting time going over this again. There's a reference here which the accused didn't refer to. Wait a moment. Let's clarify something. To the air force command of the Serb Republic of Krajina. What was that, Witness B-127, and why was that involved in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Could you say that again, the commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
