utterances.text: Just read item 5, the first paragraph. And there's a reference to the air force command of the Serbian Republic of Krajina. I wanted to know how that fits into the picture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That fits in the picture in the following way: The forces and units in Yugoslavia had cooperation established with them and so did the forces and units in the Serbian Army of Krajina. And these instructions regulate this cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it clear that this cooperation deals only with matters from item 3 of chapter 2 of these instructions? That's what it says under the heading "Application and elaboration."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in item 3 of chapter 2, we see that it only deals with exchange of information; is that correct, Mr. 127? It deals with nothing else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've been through that. We can read. And also, bear in mind don't misrepresent what the witness has said about it. Yes. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm not misquoting the witness. I'm just quoting the text. It says, "Matters from item 3, chapter 2 shall be harmonised with both parties," whereas item 3, chapter 2 deals only with exchange of information. That's what I wanted us to establish, and there's nothing more to establish, because that is the document presented by Mr. Groome here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now, tell me, please: Since Mr. Groome asked you whether we had had that type of links and exchange of information with other countries -- do you remember that question in chief? You said we didn't; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was asked was whether we had any links with some neighbouring countries like Hungary. And I said it was out of the question for military surveillance data to be handed over to Hungary. That would have been illogical. The information exchanged could only have been about civilian aviation and civilian air traffic control, and that is regulated by international rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 127, is it normal for friendly countries to exchange this type of information? Mr. Groome asked you whether we had exchanged this type of information with any other country.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a logical consequence of this to be mutually linked within Yugoslavia, but it would have been illogical to include Hungary or some other country into this system, or Croatia for that matter. And surveillance data is protected, confidential data when your aircraft are taking off. This is a very short period of time allowed for reaction. It's very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Groome asked you if we exchanged this sort of information with any other country. Do you know as an officer that the countries around us were either members of the Soviet bloc or members of NATO? So we could not have possibly exchanged this type of information with any of these.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Combat information collected through surveillance about movements within the air space is something that cannot possibly be exchanged. What we did exchange was data related to air traffic control. And to what extent a certain country is friendly or not and through what channels that goes, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But as an officer you know that we were surrounded by countries which were either members of the Soviet bloc or members of NATO, and we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. couldn't exchange this information with them, could we? And specifically here we are dealing with friendly armies, speaking about the Army of Yugoslavia and the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is your opinion, as I said. And as a matter of general principle, I can tell you again that I still feel as a Yugoslav officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is laudable. But tell me, do you possess a single report where it says -- a report of the Army of Republika Srpska where it states that it should be forwarded to the Army of Yugoslavia in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't possess any such reports, because this link established between these two levels of command we discussed earlier was automatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean that the radar pictures were visible on both sides?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And who sent reports to whom in this job, I don't know. I don't have these reports with me. But let me come back to your previous question. I was not in a position to see everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm only asking you about the things that you know. Tell me, then: Were any reports in fact sent? I assume you know that they were sent from your unit to the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, the reports are of course sent on to the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Tell me this now, please: On page 3, paragraph 3, in speaking about the increased tensions in the area of Banja Luka, you mention units of the SOS and the Wolves from Vucjak; isn't that right? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, is it true that the members of that SOS unit were exclusively people from Banja Luka and the surrounding parts? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were men who were along the battlefront in Western Slavonia or Kordun, and at one point in time they left their basic unit and arrived in Banja Luka to take over the authority there, control there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, these people who took over control, were they locals from the region, in fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly, yes. I didn't -- actually, the ones I knew were from Banja Luka and the surrounding parts. But to be quite frank, I wasn't able to identify them all myself, because it was a situation of crisis and it lasted for quite some time, and afterwards it was resolved by establishing cooperation between General Talic and the people who had a group there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it true that without exception members of those Wolves from Vucjak were also people who were locals, originated from the area? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a unit by Prnjavor and they were mostly people from the area, people who had undergone training in Knin while the Yugoslav People's Army was still in existence. And they would tell me, "We went to Captain Dragan," and I talked to these people personally, just like I'm talking to you here and now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question was: Were they locals from the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were -- they did originate from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on. We have to be more expeditious. Is it true - and you said something about this during your examination-in-chief - that before May 1992 they took control of the television transmitter near Lisina? Is that right, in Lisina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was before May 1992, and they did take control, and it was a unit of the Wolves from Vucjak, members of that unit arrived. They arrived from Knin too. And during that period of time, the television channel of Television Sarajevo was turned --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to know. And did a JNA officer - and I'm not going to read out his name, because Mr. May might tell me that this is linked to your identification or disclosing your identity, and his name isn't important - but the officer in question contacted them; isn't that right? Because he considered those people to be a danger to the unit. Is that right? That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not true that at that time, when the Yugoslav People's Army was still in existence, that those types of paramilitary, regardless of what side they were coming from. And let me say I considered them to be the paramilitary, whether they came from Croatia or whether it was a Serb paramilitary or Muslim paramilitary, and that's my position and it remains such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that he informed General Uzelac about the existence of a paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He informed the command of the Banja Luka Corps, and in cooperation with the units there was talk of having two planes take off. But they left the transmitter under threat, because they threatened to have two planes take off from the Bihac airport. And after that - just a moment, please, may I be allowed to finish - after that, the Television Belgrade channel continued to transmit programmes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I'm asking you something else. This officer informed Uzelac about this paramilitary unit, and the order arrived that they should be made to leave the transmitter on threat of having two planes take off to destroy them. And it was under this threat that they in fact relinquished control of the transmitter, and that's what you said during your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because at the time, it was an irregular unit which did not belong to the Yugoslav People's Army. Just a minute. May I be allowed to finish, please. And the possibility existed that these people would either attack the barracks and quite simply take control, take over the weaponry, so it was for security reasons that this was resorted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the JNA unit, or rather, its command issued orders that those people be made to leave, and they did leave.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, orders came from the 1st Banja Luka -- or rather, from the Banja Luka Corps, as it was called at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, tell me this, please: The relationship between the JNA and paramilitaries was quite clear -- or rather, the JNA's attitude towards the paramilitaries can be seen from that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. This was one occurrence where the situation was clear-cut, and this was a direct act by the JNA and its attitude towards this form of organisation or self-organisation for military units. So this is probably a good example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, you were present when this example was taking place, whereas you weren't present on this other occasion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was just one example. And I can't claim on the basis of one example how the JNA -- what position the JNA took with regard to the overall situation in the former Yugoslavia and vis-a-vis those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not asking you to do that either. I'm asking you to testify about things which you can testify about and which you know about. Now, please, on page 3, paragraph 4, when you speak about the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina, tell me this, please: Is it true that all the officers of the JNA, as well as the soldiers from the barracks who were from Serbia or from Macedonia or from Montenegro, for that matter, that they were returned back to their own environment? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most of the cases, that was correct, yes. But those who were in Serbia proper came to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say those who were in Serbia came to Bosnia. All that is lacking is one part; those who were in Serbia but were from Bosnia originally went to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those people who were serving in Serbia received orders to go to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you don't say that it was the Serbs from Bosnia who had gone to do their service in Serbia returned to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Serbs born in Bosnia who at that time were serving in Serbia, had employment in Serbia, received orders to go to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's just clarify this point, please. My question was this: Is it correct that all the officers of the JNA, as well as soldiers from the barracks who were from Serbia, Macedonia, and Montenegro, were returned back to their own environments? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were returned back. In most cases just the odd individual stayed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Now, during the examination-in-chief, you said that during that critical period of time - and I made a note of this, of what you said - that the non-Serbs left the army and the JNA in that area would receive -- would take on a predominantly Serb character. And that's when the Army of Republika Srpska was established. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me state that again. The Serbs who were in the JNA from Bosnia and originated from Bosnia, at the time the war broke out in Bosnia, stayed on in their units. It was the Croats and Muslims who left those units and this meant that to all intents and purposes these Serbs from Bosnia remained, and they belonged to the 30th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We'll get to the 30th Personnel Centre. You know that the Army of Republika Srpska was established at that time, and it was made up precisely of Serbs from Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's right, isn't it? And of course, there were some Muslims too, quite a large number of them, in fact, among the ranks of the Army of Republika Srpska, as well as some other nationalities and ethnic groups, but mostly they were Serbs. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Largely Serbs. As to the rest, I don't think I can agree with you that there was a large number of these others, or rather, you can mean what figure you have in mind. You can say what figure you have in mind. I would put it this way: It was a smaller number that stayed on. Now, why those people stayed on, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's common knowledge that several thousand Muslims were in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you haven't got the figure, there's no need for me to belabour the point. Now, the officers and soldiers, for example, who were from Croatia, did they leave and go to join up with the Croatian armed forces? Did the Slovenes join up with the Slovene forces, the Macedonians with the Macedonian forces, and the majority of Muslim officers joined up with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody fled every which way, back to their own parts. But the essential point is that the Croats and Muslims left the units. They left the JNA and later the Army of Republika Srpska and went to join up with those other armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, as you say that some men from Bosnia who were doing their service in Serbia or Croatia, whichever, that they received orders to join up the Army of Republika Srpska. You said that. Now, give us an example. Where did you ever see anybody receive orders in Serbia or Montenegro to join the Army of Republika Srpska, for example? Give us an example. Give me the name of at least one officer who received orders to join up with the Army of Republika Srpska. Because we have established that the citizens of Yugoslavia, when the JNA withdrew from Bosnia-Herzegovina, et cetera, and all the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as that's concerned, I didn't have occasion to see their orders or appointments. But at the start of the war, the Serbs who were doing their military service in Serbia, who were serving in the army in Serbia, came to Bosnia. Now, following what orders, on the basis of which orders, I don't know. But I think everything done in the army is based on orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, because of salaries too and the medical insurance booklets and social insurance, when it comes to a single dinar, a single penny in the army, you have to work on orders. And that is why you had this 30th Centre in the first place. I assume you're aware of that, Mr. 127. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the 30th Personnel Centre goes, it wasn't only a matter of payment and salaries. You know that there were orders pursuant to which the payments were made, and ranks were verified and certified and all the rest of it, all the other procedure that has to be gone through for each and every officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to that. We'll find all that information in due course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I'm saying is that I know what I had in my own hands and what was written in those documents. But as I say, during the war I was never in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did anybody issue you orders and order you to join up with the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until then, I was a member, an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army. Now, when the Army of Republika Srpska was established, I happened to find myself in the region, and based on those circumstances, I had to act accordingly. To tell you quite frankly, I wasn't one of those officers who left the country at the sound of the first bullet being shot. And at any rate, we went through military training for peacetime and for wartime. And at that point in time, I still sincerely believed that Yugoslavia would be a state common to us all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you on that score. You yourself said a moment ago that for the most part it was Muslims and Croats who stepped down from the JNA and left to join their own armies in their own republics. Did anybody order you to stay in the Army of Republika Srpska once it was established? You could have left, just like they had left; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I could have perhaps left. But as I say, this was risky business. It was dangerous too. And at that time, Banja Luka was closed off and even if I had wanted to leave, I was not able to do so. But let me state again: The reason I was there was as I explained it a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because you believed in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just a moment, please. May I be allowed to finish? And I state here and now, if that country were to be formed again tomorrow, the same country that existed in those previous day, I wouldn't mind losing my life for it, laying down my life for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe you there. But let's just establish some facts here, the facts that you're testifying about and that are being looked at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. here, investigated. They are taken to be some sort of evidence as to the involvement of Yugoslavia in the civil war in Bosnia. Tell me, please, Witness 127: You personally, during your officer's service in May 1992, when the Army of Republika Srpska was first formed, up until the point in time that you left the Army of Republika Srpska, during your work there, did you receive any orders from any officer of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in a unit, and I wasn't able to receive direct orders from an officer of the Army of Yugoslavia. That was the position that I was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me put it this way: Did you ever see any order issued to your unit or the command of your unit by any other command of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to that, I was present when a commander - and I'm sure you know about this - that a telegram arrived from the Army of Yugoslavia. Sir, I wasn't able to control what the commander was doing and what was in the telegram, but if that was what was said, I'm telling you what I heard and saw myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just clear that point up. What was -- what were the contents of the telegram? Why was it sent? This was all confidential, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's leave surmise and conjecture on your part to one side.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they're not assumptions. I tell you what I saw with my very own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were not familiar with the contents of that telegram to be able to claim that it was any kind of order. If you don't know the contents, then there's no need to dwell on it any further. Just tell me, please: In view of the fact that there was a war on, do you know of any situation when there was a joint military operation in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina with members of the Army of Yugoslavia taking part, a unit of the Army of Yugoslavia taking part? Just tell us whether you know of any such operation or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in view of the level of the unit that I belonged to, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you claim that the existence of the 30th Personnel Centre was actually some sort of evidence that this was a single army. Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you, regarding all the categories that qualify an officer, in those days it was a single army. That is what General Perisic himself said, after all. He was the chief of staff of the army from 1993 until 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When did he say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He stated that when he was replaced in 1998, in a magazine called "Vreme."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Probably they will be calling General Perisic to testify here, so he will be able to tell us about that. Is it true, Witness 127 -- you mentioned several times here the 30th Personnel Centre of the personnel administration of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so. We have the appropriate documents and that fictitiously the place of service is indicated as Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is there any army in the world over which a personnel administration has command? You're an educated military man.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there's no personal administration that commands, but it is a component part of the general staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that 30th Personnel Centre, did you ever receive a single order having to do with any kind of military activity from the commander of that 30th Personnel Centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the 30th Personnel Centre, Your Honour, it is a department, a personnel department of the personnel administration. There were no commanders there, except for these two men who signed those orders and -- however, all the people were either in Bosnia, and of the 40th Personnel Centre they were assigned to Croatia. We can't pretend that the 30th Personnel Centre is some kind of high-level organised structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is the whole point, Witness 127. Is it true that the 30th Personnel Centre -- before you, we had the former president of the FRY, Mr. Lilic, who explained it, because he knew it better than I did, that the 30th Personnel Centre was in one room and the 40th Personnel Centre in another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He cannot comment. He cannot comment on what some other witness has said. He doesn't know what Mr. Lilic has said and he can't comment on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness 127, is it true that the 30th Personnel Centre is no more than an administrative department in the personnel administration for those officers who used to be members of the JNA up until the 6th of April, who were employed in the JNA, and whose acquired rights to personal income, social insurance, retirement benefits remained as a form of assistance for them and their families, for those of them who had gone to join the Army of Republika Srpska and the Army of Serbian Krajina? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the 30th Personnel Centre, Your Honours, let me clear up once again. There was no one there. But the people who belonged to that 30th Personnel Centre and had all those rights in the Army of Yugoslavia, and even citizenship, were actually in Bosnia in the period from 1992 until 1995. There was a war going on in Bosnia. They were not over there -- I don't know how to put it -- taking it easy. It wasn't a hunting society.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness 127, I appreciate your humour, but the Army of Republika Srpska was officially formed and it was comprised of people who were born in Bosnia and Herzegovina, local -- the local population of Bosnia and Herzegovina; isn't that right? Regardless of whether before that they had been members of the JNA or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But at the same time, they were members of the Army of Yugoslavia. They had appointments in the Army of Yugoslavia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it clear from all the documents that Mr. Groome has produced here and which you commented upon that all those documents relate exclusively to social welfare and rights and entitlements, retirement, disability, health insurance of officers and their families, and acquired rights regarding salaries, which as material aid was granted from Yugoslavia to the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true for most of the documents. But it is important to point out here that those -- they had acquired those rights in Bosnia, as we noted a moment ago, and they realised them in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Entitlements, as you will remember, as that personnel centre existed for members of the JNA who ceased to be members of the JNA and became members of the Army of the Republika Srpska, after the 4th of May, 1992. So this was material aid to them and nothing more than that. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can define it in that way, but the procedure that existed while we were in the JNA and after that, in the Army of Republika Srpska, was identical regarding those matters, regarding material benefits. It applies to all officers in Nis or Novi Sad or anywhere else. Every officer must have an order on appointment and all these other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All those documents of the 30th Personnel Centre relate exclusively to personal incomes, their health card, booklet, retirement benefit, and social insurance; is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the order on appointment for what position he's being remunerated, and on that basis the description, his job description, his payments group, information on promotions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All of that, on the basis of the changes that occur in that individual's career by a decision of the competent bodies of the Army of Republika Srpska. But over there they administratively recorded and personal incomes provided and social insurance for them. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that is true, that everything was resolved over there. None of these matters were decided in Republika Srpska through the government of Mr. Radovan Karadzic. All these matters, as of the 6th of April onwards, until the end of the war, were decided through the Army of Yugoslavia and not through the legal government of Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The fact that you received material aid in connection with acquired rights acquired while you were members of the JNA, where your families lived, and they wouldn't have any sources of livelihood had you not received that type of aid; is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is material aid for the families. But up until the 6th of April, we had the JNA. And after the 6th of April, I'm saying, in accordance with all these documents, I was an officer of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You couldn't have been an officer of the Army of Yugoslavia and the Army of Republika Srpska, as you had your own main staff and that main staff was not subordinated to the general staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, as you know full well. Are you aware that anyone within the Army of Yugoslavia could have given an order to a single officer to go to the Army of Republika Srpska? In other words, this was left to the personal decision of each individual officer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had an example, that is, a person I spoke to, who came from Belgrade. He was serving at Banjica, to be specific. And he said to a non-commissioned officer that he had been told in Belgrade that he had been transferred to Podgorica, and as a counter-service he said, "I'd prefer to spend six months in Bosnia but to remain in Belgrade, to serve for six months in Bosnia but to remain in Belgrade."

utterances.speaker: MR. MAY
utterances.text: We've had this evidence before. The witness described that. We'll adjourn now, 20 minutes. And after that, you'll have half an hour left, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness 127, please give me brief answers, because I have very little time left and I'd like to cover as many questions as possible. Tell me, the fact that you personally through the 30th Personnel Centre were promoted to a higher rank, does that mean that someone in Belgrade had decided to promote you or was such a decision taken in the Army of Republika Srpska and only administratively processed in the 30th Personnel Centre precisely because of the amount of aid given in the form of personal income and social benefits? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours -- Your Honour, I cannot answer this question with a yes or no. These were regular promotions. After a period of three years, I get the next rank. There were no decisions by the Army of Republika Srpska. I acquired the rank on the basis of the years of service. Once a three-year period expired, then I get the next rank. I got that document from Belgrade and from no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All these documents that you produced with the stamp of the Army of Republika Srpska speak to the opposite. But let us move on. Tell me, in the 30th Personnel Centre, were there official records for any other officer of the Army of Republika Srpska except for those who used to be members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, let me respond to your remark. Judging by the dates on the documents which were doubled, first they were registered in Belgrade, then four or five months in later in Banja Luka. So the first date is in Belgrade, and then the documents from Banja Luka has the subsequent date. As for the other matter, other -- people who were in the Army of Republika Srpska and who had not served in the JNA before were not covered by the 30th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The fact that through this 30th Personnel Centre you realised your rights to health insurance, wartime service, et cetera, can this be interpreted as some sort of a commanding position of the general staff of the Army of Yugoslavia or simply as aid to a friendly army of which a number of officers had for years realised their rights in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say the following in answer to this question: Up until the 6th of April, I was an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army. After the 6th of April, judging by the documents that I had - they are my personal documents and orders - I was an officer of the Army of Yugoslavia. Now, whether this was treated by someone as aid or not, I am talking about my own documents and on the basis of what they say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. To focus on those documents. The decisions to transfer officers of the Army of Republika Srpska, were they made in Belgrade or in the Army of Republika Srpska, in Banja Luka, for instance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, regarding transfers of members of the Army of Republika Srpska --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about transfers within the Army of Republika Srpska. Who made those decisions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the Army of Republika Srpska, of course the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. No, but we referred to re-transfers. And my question regarded transfers within the Army of Republika Srpska. Tell me, the officers who used to be members of the JNA, were their records kept in the 30th Personnel Centre regarding changes in their status, payments groups, promotions, ranks, et cetera? Were these kept in the 30th administrative centre, only for them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are coming back to the same question: Who was covered by the 30th Personnel Centre? That is, the people who used to be employed in the JNA and who, upon the official withdrawal of the JNA --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you tell us where the records were kept. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All matters were regulated in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Was there any decision that was made in Belgrade or the 30th Personnel Centre only received and registered such information? That's a personnel administration; that much we established. And this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. documentation was kept in one room and related solely to salary, health insurance, and social security.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But from this application by General Talic, to be awarded status group 4, you can see clearly that he's asking for salary group or status group 4. Until then he had 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it's only about salary, this type of aid that was extended. Tell me, please, this: How many officers from the Army of Republika Srpska who used to be in the JNA left their families, children, movable and immovable property in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you specify? You mean non-Serbs or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about people who joined the Army of Republika Srpska, they had families, these families have to live somehow, be they in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or in Republika Srpska, in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's true that certain members of the 30th Personnel Centre had families in the Army of Yugoslavia, and it is -- it was normal for these people to receive salaries if they were employed -- if their father or husband was employed in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they were members of the Army of Republika Srpska and they were born in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. They were members of the Army of Republika Srpska. They belonged also to the 30th Personnel Centre of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we're talking about only a personnel administration which cared for your pensionable service and your health insurance, and you addressed them concerning everything that had to do with your years of service; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You really have exhausted this topic. We have been round and round it. We've heard the evidence. We have the documentation in front of us, and it will be for us to make our minds up. There's no point arguing any further with the witness about it. If you'd like to move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'm not arguing with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it disputed, then, that this was only a form of material aid between two friendly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That will be a matter for us to determine in due course. It's not for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well, Mr. May. I wanted to hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is there any other document issuing orders on the part of the Army of Yugoslavia that does not relate to social entitlements and salary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We have been over this, so move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say -- in fact, do you know for how long was this aid extended? Until 2000 or 2001? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And just a second. Your Honours, let us make one distinction. We are talking about different forms of interruption in financing, sending of orders, and other administrative issues for different categories of persons. If we start from the bottom, contractual soldiers in the Army of Republika Srpska who belonged there, as far as these people are concerned, that was settled in 1994. As for civilians employed in the army who were later renamed workers in the Army of Republika Srpska, who also belonged to the 30th Personnel Centre, that was settled somewhere in 1997. And the last came officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean in 2000 and 2001. That means that aid continued for all of seven years after the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, is it clear, then, that this aid had nothing to do with the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That aid started when the war broke out and lasted as long as it lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the war ended in 1995, and for seven years after that you continued to receive that same aid and it did not serve the purpose of waging war. Is it clear that this has nothing to do with anything else except for salary and social security?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, during the war, appointments were made according to wartime establishment and double credit was given for years of service; whereas, after the war, appointments of officers were made according to peacetime establishment and they also belonged to the same 30th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In answer to the question as to the aid ending, the aid continued for all of seven years after the war; is that correct? And you said, "Yes, it is." And you were going on to say something else when you were interrupted. Now, is there anything else you want to add to explain that? If you've answered the question, don't worry. That's fine. But if there's anything you want to add, then it's your opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wish to add this: On this point, I'd like to say these issues are very complex. You cannot answer yes or no, because when we discuss the war from 1992 until 1995, we have to bear in mind all those who were left behind us, and we are here probably to show the truth about what happened there, to prevent future generations to look for reasons and causes in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us just stick to the point, shall we? Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Anything more you want to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is not disputed that this aid continued for seven years after the war, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not disputed. All I'm telling you is that you interpret it as aid, and I see it as a member of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What -- when did this 30th personnel detachment, when did that come to an end, its activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was interpreted to me as "detachment," in the military sense. The 30th Personnel Centre, military post 3001, terminated its activities in 2000 and all the people who were born in Bosnia continued to receive their salaries from then on from the Army of Republika Srpska. I mentioned earlier that contracted soldiers and other categories were taken off the payroll of the 30th Personnel Centre much earlier, in 1994 and 1997. I don't know why it was handled that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We'll hear that from another witness who is more qualified. But it is undisputed that until year 2000, and perhaps later, this aid continued, linked to some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, he's not talked about aid. It's you who uses that expression. All he's talking about is the activities of this personnel centre and the activities of officers who were fighting in Bosnia but paid for by the Army of Yugoslavia. That's the point. Now, what the significance of that is is for us to determine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Well, as for the significance of all that, since the witness asserts that this link -- in fact, the existence of the 30th Personnel Centre is evidence that this was a single army and, according to him, it lasted until the year 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's undisputed; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not disputed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that that single army, if it were a single army, continued to exist until the NATO aggression. Did the Army of Republika Srpska take part in the defence against the NATO aggression?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To that question, I'll answer that as far as I know, there was no active participation of the Army of Republika Srpska in terms of extending any significant assistance to the Army of Yugoslavia. Apart from that, the Army of Republika Srpska was under the direct control of SFOR, and it is very difficult to imagine any assistance they would have been able to give at that moment. There was a number of inspections carried out by SFOR in all barracks throughout Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Witness. But if it had been a single army and you know that there were activities against Yugoslavia from the territory of Republika Srpska, then if it had been a single army, it would have been acted against the aggressor, on the side of Yugoslavia. Isn't that evidence that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's all a matter of argument. You can make those submissions to us. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any unit of the Army of Republika Srpska even before the NATO aggression that was used in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking from my level, I don't know whether any unit was used in Kosovo. But as for Kosovo, in that period - I emphasise, in 1996 - first IFOR came and then SFOR, and the area was under the direct control of SFOR in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how was your function different? Because you received your salaries from that personnel centre. How was it different? How was the situation different until 1995 from the period after 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until 1996, we had official IDs of the Army of Republika Srpska. And the only difference is that the period we spent in the war is the period for which we received double credit, in terms of pensionable service. And later on we were a peacetime establishment, and later on we had official IDs of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your IDs are your own personal matter. I'm telling you that the function was the same from 1992 until 2001. A larger part of this period was after the war, and there was no difference in terms of salary and social entitlements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the question? There's no point telling him anything; you must ask him questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the difference in the treatment and status of this 30th Personnel Centre before the war and after the war? It's obvious there's no difference.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. As far as the way we were treated is concerned, there is a difference. We were -- we received double credit for the wartime period and later on we received years of service one-for-one, as a peacetime formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Witness 127. You mentioned -- there is one document, and since my time is short, I cannot go through even a small part of the documents produced here, but let us take just a few. The application of General Galic for recognition of his entitlement to salary group 4, and the verification of his rank of colonel. This has to do with his retirement and social security entitlements. Take this paper. The last numbers are 831. You answered in response to one question by Mr. Groome that promotions were given in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Prosecution to clarify, Exhibit 505.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's tab 10 of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, look now. It discusses solely this: Correction of the calculation of entitlements and recognition of -- and then the second paragraph says: "It is evident from our personnel records and the decree of the president of Republika Srpska on his appointment that the above named has" and so on and so forth. So the general in question, General Galic, was appointed by a decree of the president of Republika Srpska, and he is registered herein and he was receiving this aid, in terms of salary and social security rights, and these security rights need to be settled, regulated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: My microphone is out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The microphone is on again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it clear from this, because it says, "It is evident from our personnel records and the decree of the president of Republika Srpska," is it clear that he was appointed by the decree of the president of the Republika Srpska and no one in the Army of Yugoslavia? Is it clear or not? Tell me, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document talks about promotion, in view of goals achieved and attainments of the general in question, in view of which he was promoted by the organs of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for one moment, please. Does the final paragraph of that document refer to taking all the necessary steps within your authority to confirm the said officer's rank to which he was promoted by the responsible superior officer in conformity with the applicable regulations of the Army of Yugoslavia? Does it say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely what I meant to say. President Radovan Karadzic was able to promote somebody into the rank of general if he had a rank of colonel in the 30th Personnel Centre. But until it is verified, according to regulations of the Army of Yugoslavia, he remains a colonel for the purposes of the 30th Personnel Centre, and that is why this application is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it clear that the only matter in question here is that criteria applicable in the Army of Yugoslavia concerning salary, retirement entitlements, et cetera, need to be respected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing clear from this is that it has to be adjusted to the applicable regulations of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if that is so, let me ask you to come back to the first paragraph. They say they want an amendment of the decision of the military social insurance fund for his old-age pension to be calculated and the rank of lieutenant general. So it relates only to social security issues. They should be applied the same as in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, Your Honours, relates to a man who is already Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. retired. This is an application for him to receive a higher payment group, four instead of six. Probably until then he was in group six, and it has to do with his pension that he was receiving.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it's a social entitlement that is in question here, nothing else. Is that disputed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is about his pension because he wasn't receiving the correct remuneration. But it is settled in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've now exhausted this topic. You've got four minutes left, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, then, before I move on to another area, I should just like to draw your attention to the following: Dates are very important here. Now, it says 4/4081, that document, the regulation for Yugoslav citizenship, and this refers to 1997. That's the date. And it speaks about regulations on the basis of which citizens who do not enjoy Yugoslav citizenship can acquire it. And no differentiation is made between those who were members of the army from other citizens of Republika Srpska; is that quite clear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I take a look at that document, please, for me to be able to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we can read it all ourselves. Thank you very much. Let's -- let's move on to something else, and then you can come to an end, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, is this next document quite clear, the one that relates to the command of the 503rd Motorised Brigade? And you yourself said that that was the Army of Republika Srpska, and the man's name was Dragan Obrenovic. And it gives us the date, which was the 1st --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have the document. It's the same tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Tab 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's tab 11, in fact. Yes, quite right. It's the third document in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to enter into any details, because I haven't got time for that, but is the date the 1st of February, 1999? Is that right? And then it goes on to determine a deputy for the 503rd Motorised Brigade, and the date there is the 29th of September, 1998; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I have here is a document, 6839 are the final digits of the number of that document -- yes, that's right. It does refer to 1999, the 1st of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The 1st of February, 1999. That's right. And a representative for the 503rd Motorised Brigade is the 29th of September, 1998; that's the date. So all these are documents after the war, and the procedure is the same as it was during the war and refers exclusively to social entitlements. Is that quite clear or not, Witness 127?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when the previous question was asked and when the accused referred to citizens, that it only referred to citizens who could regulate their nationality status in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia - that's what that was about - that was a document received by the corps command. And there is no question there of it referring to citizens. All it refers to is members of the 30th Personnel Centre, stipulating that they will be able to solve their citizenship status within the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, there is no obligation to grant anybody's citizenship, and the first paragraph of that letter states, "On the basis of the law governing Yugoslav citizenship," and then in brackets "Official Gazette of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, 1996, with the aim of realising these rights," et cetera, et cetera. So the explanation given is how pursuant to the law --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to go through this. Now, would you please answer the question shortly, Witness B-127. You've got two more questions left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If he's answered the question, in your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And we're talking about the year 1997. And explanations are provided and information as to how to acquire Yugoslav citizenship pursuant to the law stipulated in the Official Gazette of Yugoslavia, I don't assume that is in dispute, Witness 127.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Two more questions, Mr. Milosevic, and hurry up with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's very difficult for me to make a selection from all of this here, Mr. May. But I'll leave behind this pile of regulations and I'd just like to draw your attention to the pile of documents, in fact, where we can see that 1999, 1997, 1998, those years, that that's what it refers to and that there's nothing different there to what it was 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, let me just ask you one more thing in connection with what you said during your examination-in-chief, about the destruction of the mosque in Banja Luka between the 7th and 8th of May, 1993, in fact. I'm sure you'll remember that, having said that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know, are you aware, that it was from the top of the Republika Srpska, with Radovan Karadzic's signature, that after this sabotage an order was issued for the police to protect all religious sites in Banja Luka? Are you aware of that? Just give me a yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but I do know that all the mosques in Banja Luka were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about in Serbia? Was a single mosque destroyed in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, that did not happen. Nothing like that happened over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And when you spoke about the destruction of the Catholic church in Banja Luka in 1995, you said that this took place after the fall of Krajina and that it was destroyed as a form of revenge, revanchism is what you said. That's what you said during your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it wasn't Krajina. I said with the fall of Western Slavonia. That's what I said. Several days after that was when the mining of the Catholic monastery took place when it was blown up next to Banja Luka. And that was a terrible thing too, regardless of what religious site we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 127, I'm not saying that it isn't a terrible thing. I'm just saying that you said that this was after the fall -- all right. Let me say Western Slavonia. You put me right there. I wrote down "Krajina," but all right, Western Slavonia, that this was a form of revanchism. Now, do you know how many dozens of thousands of people, refugees, at that time flowed into that area and passed through Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you say, sir, is correct. However -- and that's an unfortunate circumstance. It's a sad thing that that happened, and I say that before this court. But do you know, sir, how many in Banja Luka, people at that same period of time, were expelled, expelled onto the streets?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must really bring this to an end. Yes. Have the amici any questions? And if you could, be as expeditious as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll try and be expeditious. I'd like to ask the witness to explain to you several points in relation to the documents found in tab 12 and 14. One is dated the 28th of July, 1994; that's tab 12, a decision. And second is a document dated the 5th of October, 1994. So could we refer to those documents and put them before the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This first document bears the number in the English translation 0084022, and the next ERN number is for the B/C/S version. It is a document signed by Strbac, the commander, military commander from Zvornik. Have you got that? The 28th of July is the date.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 28th of July, 1994? Yes, I do have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, take a look at this certificate issued by the military authorities of the Army of Republika Srpska. That's right, isn't it? That's the certificate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And it was signed by Strbac; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And this is a certificate certifying to the following, that Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, a resident of Zvornik, member of the Army of Republika Srpska, was wounded on the 28th of August, 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And a description of the event follows and how he was injured. And he said, "On the 29th of August, 1992, in the region of Zaglovka [phoen] in Visegrad, during attack operations, he stepped on a buried anti-tank mine, which is how he was injured, Colonel [interpretation inaudible], and then it says the injury he incurred, the lumbar part of the spinal column and the heel." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So it is combat operations that are mentioned here; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that the person in question, lieutenant colonel, was wounded and that a certificate is being issued to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm interested in this section where it says "attack operations," "combat operations."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So this kind of document could not have been issued by anybody else but by the representatives of the military authorities, because nobody had information about combat operations of this kind at the cadre centre in Belgrade; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the combat operations go and information about that, at the 30th Personnel Centre, in my own opinion - and let me say again that I was never there throughout the war for me to be able to speak about combat operations and what they had over there - but in my opinion, they did not have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, for anybody to enjoy rights pursuant to that, he would have to have been issued a certificate of this kind, on the basis of information they had. And this could only be issued by representatives of the powers that be in Republika Srpska. It wasn't something that the people had who were working in the Army of Yugoslavia. They did not dispose of any such information; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. This is a certificate, which is being issued for the member of the army of the republic to enjoy certain rights. So the possibility exists that this certificate could directly be used in Republika Srpska. I don't know who this was addressed to or sent to, whether to the 30th Personnel Centre or to some municipality or the like for the allotment of an apartment or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand all that. That's not what I'm asking you. But I'm interested in this second certificate of the 5th of October, performed assignments in the zone of combat operations. Now, the information on combat operations and wartime situations in Republika Srpska, this is something that only the authorities of Republika Srpska would know about; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information about combat operations, yes, that was established exclusively in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have just one more thing to ask you in respect of these documents, about the promotions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. May I be allowed to add something and to give examples? This was a specific form of a unit. May I clarify what "combat operation" means for -- as related to a unit? This is the activities of a unit, whether it uncovers any aircraft flying overhead, that is incorporated into combat assignment. It all comes under the heading of combat operation or assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that will be up to Their Honours to decide. But I'm interested in the documents dating back to 1992, 1993, 1994, and 1995, compiled by the personnel centre. Now, are those all matters which within the frameworks of the military service were subordinated to the general staff of the Army of Yugoslavia at that time and the Supreme Commander? Did it all come under them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not receiving the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my final question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The documents you spoke about, up until 1995, until the end of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were they compiled and issued within the frameworks of military authorities under supervision and control of the general staff of the Army of Yugoslavia at that time and the Supreme Commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says as a header, "The general staff personnel administration," and what the document refers to. That is stated in the header. Whether it's an order of appointment, a job description, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Page 80 on line 15 of the transcript I believe records a translation error. It records you as saying the follow: Until 1996 we had official IDs of the Army of Republika Srpska. Can I ask you just to briefly state, prior to 1996, what identification did you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, until 1996, it was the identification cards of the Yugoslav People's Army that were in force, which means throughout that period -- I'm not hearing anything. I can't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you hear me now? My next question to you is: Mr. Milosevic asked you about the circumstances surrounding how you came to be a witness here today. I'm going to ask that the following document be assigned an exhibit number. I'm going ask you to look at it. It is the English translation of a letter. I'm going to ask you: Do you recognise the content of this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. letter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recognise the content of the letter. It is my document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you send a letter to the Prosecutor, informing her that you had information to provide relevant to this particular case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And as I said at the outset, I took the first step towards the contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're still in the process of trying to locate the original written in the witness's hand. I would tender this exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, number 505, tab 18, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the accused put the document 505, tab 4 and suggested to you that all this document deals with is exclusively the change of information. On the screen in front of you, I've asked that a -- a portion of that document be displayed. It's item 3. Can I ask you to simply read the last item in number 3, the very bottom item in that section.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It says here: "The elaboration of joint plans, the use of forces, and the elaboration of coordinated action plans." And I add also an exchange of information in the civilian section. That is probably something that is quite ordinary, exchange of information collected for this form, these units, is considered a combat operation or activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When it refers to the deployment of forces, is that referring to something outside the units that you were involved in and you were a part of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does the document that we have before us, does it refer to other plans and deployment of forces -- does it refer to other matters outside of those directly dealt with with this particular document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It refers, among other things, to the exchange of officers for coordinated action in command posts and operation centres of commands and units, exchange of data regarding the situation in the air space, what they -- what we see that they should see and vice versa. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this is an order approved by General Mladic, and it purports to give direction to the VRS, members of the VJ, and members of the SVK. Can you explain under what circumstances General Mladic would be able to issue such an order that would be binding upon those other two armies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Groome is phrasing the question incorrectly, because General Mladic, in this document, is not giving any orders to the Army of Yugoslavia or to the Serbian Army of Krajina. On the contrary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can read it. We can read it. Now, let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander, General Mladic, was commander of the Army of Republika Srpska. And these were plans of coordinated actions. But it's not an order. These are instructions in view of the newly created situation; what certain levels of units should do in certain situations, what should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My last question to you -- and I would ask that the witness be shown once again tab 12 of Exhibit 505. It's the document ending in 0095, marked with the blue tag. You've discussed this document before, and this is the extraordinary promotion of Vinko Pandurevic and Dragan Obrenovic. You have touched upon the circumstances surrounding when somebody might be extraordinarily promoted. Can I ask you, in a clear, concise sentence, to explain to the Chamber what is an extraordinary promotion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, so this is an extraordinary promotion, which means that it is premature for certain activities. Pandurevic Vinko, and Obrenovic Dragan are being promoted, and it is clearly stated that they are serving in the 30th Personnel Centre of the general staff of the Yugoslav army. The date of the promotion is indicated, certified by military post, indicating the location which is Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, it's a matter of public record that Vinko Pandurevic was indicted for crimes he's alleged to have committed in July of 1995, and it's also a matter of public record that Mr. Dragan Obrenovic recently pled guilty to those same crimes in July 1995. What is the date from this document when they were promoted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is, on the basis of the order of the 31st of December, 1995, and it is recorded or registered on the 6th of January, 1996. So the order was written on the 31st of December, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness B-127, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go, but would you just wait a moment until the blinds are closed. After this witness is concluded, there are some rulings which I want to give.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Prosecution can please clarify which tabs should be under seal. I currently have tab 1, tab 3, tab 5, tab 6, tab 7, tab 8, tab 18, with tab 16 being withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I gather the next witness is protected. It really is important that we deal with these matters expeditiously. Now, we can have the witness in while the blinds are down, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to propose that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But it's important that these rulings be given. They're in your interest, if I may say, because they relate to the Prosecution evidence. How long will it take to get the next witness here? Well, let's have the next witness here and we'll make a start, five to ten minutes of the evidence, and then we'll break off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any other administrative matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A couple of administrative matters and then about the witness in closed session, briefly. Preparing for the three-week break, not knowing how we can most assist the Chamber and its staff, I can tell you that we are in a position to provide you by the end of next week with up-to-date chronology and an up-to-date fillbox documents of the type you've seen before, if that would be of assistance to the Chamber. We've also in mind this spirit of the recent rule change, and we'll try and provide maps for both Croatia and Bosnia by next week which will show which particular locations have been covered by evidence and which locations have had partial evidence cover, because it seems to us that might be something helpful for us all to be able to see pictorially as well as to have listed in another way. I'll provide a new witness list, probably tomorrow or the day after, which will indicate the further cuts we've made and the amount of time we have yet further to cut to meet the deadline. As to the order of witnesses, the present list proposes B-083, followed by another 92 bis -- by a 92 bis witness, and then Audrey Budding, the historian. I would seek to take Audrey Budding immediately after B-083, for various reasons, not the least because she comes from further much away, she's an expert, and it's always desirable to keep the experts here, for various reasons, as short a period of time as possible, so that I would hope she would be in a position to start tomorrow, and that the accused would be ready for that. He would have been ready for her tomorrow, in any event, I think. I shall be taking this witness briefly in chief, as I do with all experts. The Chamber will recall that we had provisionally made a decision that we -- although we wanted a historian, we would nevertheless be able to do without her in view of the pressures of time on us. The same day as we were about to announce that decision, the Chamber expressed its view that there should be a historian available, and so she's here. But we would very respectfully invite the Chamber to consider in pressing the accused to focus his cross-examination rather than to explore everything, focus on matters that are really in dispute, with her. But I shall probably take her for less than half an hour in chief, I would hope. As to this witness, B-083, can I address you briefly about him in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
